ECE 6612

Email domain authentication

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows two aligned authentication routes that can support a message’s visible From domain.

An incoming message names several identities. The SMTP envelope sender receives delivery reports. The visible From header claims the author shown to the reader. A DKIM signature names a signing domain. The receiver also observes the connecting SMTP peer’s IP address. Domain-authentication checks begin by selecting the identity they actually evaluate.

Sender Policy Framework (SPF) evaluates the connecting peer IP against the envelope-sender domain’s DNS TXT policy, or the HELO identity in applicable cases. Mechanisms such as ip4 and include can match that IP. The matching mechanism’s qualifier gives pass (+), fail (-), softfail (~), or neutral (?). A final -all produces fail when no earlier mechanism matched. The receiver then uses that evidence in its handling policy.

DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) signs selected message headers and body data. In a DKIM-Signature header, d= names the signing domain and s= selects a key. The lookup is selector._domainkey.signing-domain. The receiver retrieves the public key, checks the covered body hash bh= and verifies b= under the declared algorithm and canonicalization rules. Coverage fields such as h= identify signed headers. The evidence applies to those covered data under the signing domain.

Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) connects a passing identity with the visible From domain through alignment. Let S mean SPF passes, Aₛ mean its envelope domain aligns, D mean a DKIM signature passes, and Aᴅ mean that signature’s domain aligns. Then DMARC pass = (S AND Aₛ) OR (D AND Aᴅ). Strict alignment requires exact domain agreement. Relaxed alignment can accept subdomains sharing the applicable organizational domain.

The receiver looks up the visible From domain’s DMARC policy at _dmarc.domain, applying the protocol’s fallback rules where relevant. A policy can request none, quarantine or reject for failures, and rua can request aggregate reporting. Authentication, alignment, requested handling and the receiver’s final disposition are separate stages. A domain authorized to send mail can still send harmful content, so domain evidence supports spoofing assessment alongside content and reputation checks.

Forwarding changes the connecting peer IP and can therefore break SPF for the original envelope identity. DKIM can survive when the covered data stay intact; a mailing list’s body or header edits can break it. A valid signature can also accompany a replay. Each receiving server prepends a Received header, placing the newest hop first. The current receiver directly observed its immediate peer; older trace lines depend on trust in the systems that supplied them.

Spam filtering combines evidence about content, behavior, reputation and authenticated domains. Provider controls and legal accountability address other stages of abuse. A protocol pass establishes its specific identity claim, while the user-facing safety decision also depends on what the message asks the recipient to do.

Example

A message displays From: billing@shop.example, uses envelope bounce@mailer.example, and carries a valid DKIM signature with d=shop.example. SPF passes for mailer.example but lacks alignment with shop.example. The exactly aligned DKIM pass supplies the DMARC passing route. If a forwarder later changes the signed body, DKIM may fail and the receiver must recompute the available routes.

Sources and scope
  • C18 Email Security: envelope/header identities, SPF, DKIM, DMARC, forwarding, trace headers and spam controls.
  • RFC 7208: SPF; RFC 6376: DKIM; RFC 7489: DMARC.
  • C18 closing spam/provider/legal material is supported by the November 10 lecture recording.

Practice

1. Visible From is alerts@example.com. SPF passes for bounce@dispatch.example.net. DKIM passes with d=mail.example.com. With relaxed alignment, does DMARC pass? What changes under strict alignment?

Compute pass and alignment together for each route; use the visible From domain as the comparison target.

Under relaxed alignment, the DKIM signing domain mail.example.com shares organizational domain example.com with visible From, so the DKIM route passes and aligns. SPF’s example.net identity is unrelated. Under strict alignment the DKIM domain differs from example.com, so neither route supplies an aligned pass and DMARC fails, assuming no other passing signature.

2. A forwarder preserves signed message data but sends from a new IP. Explain which authentication input changes and which can remain valid.

SPF follows the current SMTP peer; DKIM follows covered message data.

The next receiver observes the forwarder’s IP, which may fall outside the original envelope domain’s SPF policy. DKIM can still verify if the signature and all required covered data remain valid. The receiver then tests alignment of any passing identity with visible From and applies its handling policy.
